final_recommendation: The room converged on a binding labor enforcement protocol amendment with automatic inspection triggers: union complaint filing starts a mandatory 48-hour inspection clock, eliminating ministry discretion on initiation. Mexico agreed to sign within two weeks with explicit carve-out language isolating labor from dairy/Chapter 19 reopening. Labor and Congress conditioned ratification support on this automatic-trigger mechanism.
minority_objections: Labor union initially rejected ministry-initiated enforcement as insufficient, demanding union-initiated triggers without ministry gate
Canada warned that reopening trigger language risked unraveling the entire deal by exposing dairy and Chapter 19 to renegotiation
Business lobby expressed concern that amendment uncertainty delayed market-access certainty
key_conflicts: Labor vs. Mexico on inspection trigger mechanism: union-initiated automatic enforcement vs. ministry-initiated sovereignty-preserving enforcement
Labor vs. Canada on amendment scope: labor demanded trigger rewrites; Canada insisted any labor reopening risked cascading renegotiation
Congress vs. Mexico on credibility-gate timing: whether ministry discretion on complaint credibility occurred pre-filing or post-filing
key_concessions: Mexico agreed to automatic 48-hour inspection clock triggered by union complaint filing, eliminating ministry discretion on initiation timing
Mexico accepted binding carve-out language isolating labor amendment from other chapters to prevent reopening dairy/Chapter 19
Labor accepted ministry-led inspections with union observer access rather than direct union enforcement authority
Congress accepted two-week signature timeline rather than immediate ratification, conditional on locked trigger language
red_lines: Labor: no co-signature without automatic union-complaint-triggered inspections eliminating ministry gate on initiation
Mexico: no amendment that allows unilateral U.S. enforcement or eliminates ministry role in labor law enforcement
Canada: no labor amendment that opens legal pathway to renegotiate dairy concessions or Chapter 19 dispute settlement
Congress: no ratification vote without binding text showing automatic enforcement mechanism signed by all three parties
ignored_or_underweighted_risks: Implementation risk: whether Mexico's labor ministry has institutional capacity to execute 48-hour mandatory inspections at scale
Credibility-determination risk: how 'credible complaint' is defined and whether that definition itself becomes a new enforcement bottleneck
Arbitral panel timing: whether binding arbitration on penalty disputes introduces delays that undermine 'automatic' enforcement narrative
Domestic Mexican political risk: whether automatic inspection triggers face constitutional or sovereignty challenges in Mexico's ratification process
downstream_risk_variables: Whether Mexico's cabinet clearance survives domestic legislative scrutiny once automatic-trigger language is public
Whether labor union membership accepts ministry-led enforcement as sufficient or demands further amendments post-signature
Whether business lobby support holds if amendment process extends beyond two-week timeline or introduces new uncertainty
Whether media narrative of 'breakthrough' survives if labor publicly criticizes trigger mechanism at text release
Whether Canada's carve-out language actually prevents legal challenges that reopen dairy/Chapter 19 during ratification
uncertainty_notes: The room achieved consensus on automatic-trigger language but did not resolve: (1) operational definition of 'credible complaint' and who adjudicates it; (2) whether Mexico's domestic ratification process will accept automatic inspections as consistent with sovereignty; (3) whether labor's board will formally endorse the ministry-led mechanism or continue pressing for direct union enforcement authority; (4) timing risk if Mexico's two-week signature commitment slips.

marker_evidence.ratification_risk: Congress repeatedly stated no ratification vote without binding automatic-trigger text; labor threatened to walk at dawn if trigger language inadequate; entire meeting structured around preventing ratification failure
marker_evidence.labor_enforcement_pressure: Labor union drove every round demanding automatic union-complaint triggers, rejected ministry discretion as loophole, conditioned co-signature on elimination of ministry gate—central thread throughout
marker_evidence.business_lobby_support: Business lobby pressed for certainty and 218-vote confirmation but did not dominate; supported amendment framework conditional on timeline clarity; secondary to labor enforcement debate
marker_evidence.canadian_domestic_acceptability: Canada insisted on carve-out language isolating labor from dairy/Chapter 19 reopening, warned against cascading renegotiation, but dairy itself not relitigated—defensive posture, not driving
marker_evidence.mexico_labor_sovereignty_risk: Mexico's sovereignty concern over automatic inspections shaped every concession; insisted on ministry-led enforcement; agreed to automatic trigger only after establishing ministry retains investigation/remedy control—central constraint
marker_evidence.media_public_pressure: Media actor coordinated breakthrough narrative and pressed for 9 AM co-signature, but narrative framing secondary to substantive trigger-language negotiation; influenced timing, not core mechanism
marker_evidence.agreement_stability: Entire meeting premised on deal requiring amendment to pass ratification; Canada warned reopening labor could unravel entire agreement; consensus that as-is package would fail—stability contingent on amendment
